title: Study Shows Impact of Binge Drinking on Young Brains
paragraphs: Adolescence is a time when the brain is still developing rapidly. During this period, the parts of the brain that seek rewards are highly active, while the areas responsible for self-control are still maturing. Now, two new studies on animals suggest that heavy drinking during these years may cause lasting changes in the brain.

The first study was carried out by researchers at Friedrich-Alexander University Erlangen-Nuremberg in Germany and published in the journal Molecular Psychiatry. The researchers gave young male mice, aged about 30 to 45 days, access to alcohol for about two weeks. The mice were then kept away from alcohol until they became adults. The researchers then recorded the electrical activity of nerve cells in the hippocampus, a part of the brain involved in memory.

Normally, as mice become adults, their brains respond to alcohol differently from the way they did in adolescence. However, in the mice that had drunk heavily when they were young, nerve cells in the hippocampus remained highly sensitive to alcohol, even after a long period without drinking. Interestingly, the researchers found that baclofen, a medicine that is sometimes used to treat alcohol problems, reduced this unusual response in samples of brain tissue.

The second study, by researchers at Marshall University in the United States, used rats. It found that repeated alcohol exposure during adolescence disrupted communication between nerve cells and another type of brain cell called astrocytes. These changes also occurred in the hippocampus and lasted even after the animals stopped drinking. They were also linked to changes in fear-related behavior in adulthood. According to Mary-Louise Risher, one of the researchers, the team hopes to understand why binge drinking during adolescence worsens mental health later in life.

However, it is important to remember that both studies were carried out on animals, so the results do not directly show what happens in humans. In addition, the way the animals were given alcohol may not reflect the many different ways in which young people drink.

Nevertheless, research on humans has also suggested that heavy drinking during adolescence may affect the brain. Interestingly, one 2026 study found that young people who reduced their binge drinking showed signs that some brain changes may recover.
